claim: Continuous exposure to natural blends of herbivore-induced volatiles results in clocked temporal response patterns in neighboring plants, characterized by an induced terpene burst at the onset of the second day of exposure.
source: Using a custom-built, high-throughput proton transfer reaction time-of-flight mass spectrometry (PTR-ToF-MS) system, we explored temporal patterns of volatile transfer and responses between herbivore-attacked and undamaged maize plants. We found that continuous exposure to natural blends of herbivore-induced volatiles results in clocked temporal response patterns in neighboring plants, characterized by an induced terpene burst at the onset of the second day of exposure.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from PTR-ToF-MS measurements showing temporal patterns of volatile responses.

claim: The delayed terpene burst is not explained by terpene accumulation during the night.
source: This delayed burst is not explained by terpene accumulation during the night, but coincides with delayed jasmonate accumulation in receiver plants.
evidence: The claim is supported by measurements of internal terpene pools showing they remain comparable between night and day.

claim: The delayed terpene burst coincides with delayed jasmonate accumulation in receiver plants.
source: This delayed burst is not explained by terpene accumulation during the night, but coincides with delayed jasmonate accumulation in receiver plants.
evidence: The claim is supported by phytohormone measurements showing jasmonate induction at 22 hours.

claim: The delayed burst occurs independent of day:night light transitions.
source: The delayed burst occurs independent of day:night light transitions and cannot be fully explained by sender volatile dynamics.
evidence: The claim is supported by continuous light experiments showing similar delayed burst patterns.

claim: The delayed burst cannot be fully explained by sender volatile dynamics.
source: The delayed burst occurs independent of day:night light transitions and cannot be fully explained by sender volatile dynamics.
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis showing bioactive volatile emissions from sender plants do not fully explain receiver plant responses under continuous light.

claim: The delayed burst is the result of a stress memory from volatile exposure during the first day and secondary exposure to bioactive volatiles on the second day.
source: Instead, it is the result of a stress memory from volatile exposure during the first day and secondary exposure to bioactive volatiles on the second day.
evidence: The claim is supported by experiments showing that short HIPV exposure followed by HAC treatment the next day produces enhanced terpene responses.

claim: Prolonged exposure to natural blends of stress-induced volatiles results in a response that integrates priming and direct induction into a distinct and predictable temporal response pattern.
source: Our study reveals that prolonged exposure to natural blends of stress-induced volatiles results in a response that integrates priming and direct induction into a distinct and predictable temporal response pattern.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing both priming effects and direct induction occurring sequentially.

claim: Plants rely on chemical cues to identify and mount appropriate responses to herbivores.
source: Plants rely on chemical cues to identify and mount appropriate responses to herbivores (Waterman et al., 2019; Escobar-Bravo et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: When perceived by undamaged plants, HIPVs can enhance plant defenses, and thus increase plant resistance to future herbivory.
source: When perceived by undamaged plants, HIPVs can enhance plant defenses, and thus increase plant resistance to future herbivory (Erb et al., 2015; Kalske et al., 2019; Hu et al., 2019; Engelberth et al., 2004; Vázquez-González et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: HIPVs can directly induce plant defenses.
source: HIPVs can directly induce plant defenses (Hu et al., 2019; Engelberth et al., 2004; Wang et al., 2023; Ruther and Fürstenau, 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: HIPVs can prime plant defenses, where HIPV-exposed plants respond more strongly and/or more rapidly to a secondary stimulus such as herbivore attack.
source: HIPVs can also prime plant defenses. In this case, HIPV-exposed plants respond more strongly and/or more rapidly to a secondary stimulus such as herbivore attack (Erb et al., 2015; Hu et al., 2019; Engelberth et al., 2004; Mauch-Mani et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Artificial herbivory that mimics spatiotemporal patterns of chewing herbivores induces more a similar response to actual herbivore attack than when spatiotemporal patterns are ignored.
source: For example, artificial herbivory that mimics spatiotemporal patterns of chewing herbivores induces more a similar response to actual herbivore attack than when spatiotemporal patterns are ignored (Mithöfer et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The emission of HIPVs follows discrete temporal dynamics.
source: The emission of HIPVs also follows discrete temporal dynamics (Erb et al., 2015; Yu et al., 2017), which, again, is likely to influence defense responses in receiver plants.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Green leaf volatiles are catabolic products of the lipoxygenase/hydroperoxide lyase pathway and are emitted within minutes following damage.
source: Green leaf volatiles (GLVs), including (Z)-3-hexenyl acetate (HAC), (Z)-3-hexenal, and (Z)-3-hexen-1-ol, are catabolic products of the lipoxygenase/hydroperoxide lyase pathway and are emitted within minutes following damage (D'Auria et al., 2007; Matsui, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Indole and terpenes are emitted within hours of herbivore attack.
source: Indole and terpenes are emitted within hours of herbivore attack (Escobar-Bravo et al., 2023; Erb et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Indole can mediate interactions between plants as well as between plants and other organisms.
source: Indole can mediate interactions between plants as well as between plants and other organisms (Ye et al., 2021; Ye et al., 2018; Veyrat et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Terpenes are a very diverse group of volatiles (>80,000 known structures) that are important as both direct and indirect plant defenses.
source: Terpenes are a very diverse group of volatiles (>80,000 known structures) that are also important as both direct and indirect plant defenses (Kalske et al., 2019; Chen et al., 2021; Zhou and Pichersky, 2020; Riedlmeier et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Indole and terpenes take longer to produce in comparison to GLVs and are less transiently emitted.
source: Indole and terpenes take longer to produce in comparison to GLVs and are less transiently emitted (Escobar-Bravo et al., 2023; Erb et al., 2015; D'Auria et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: In maize, GLVs have been implicated in direct induction.
source: In maize, GLVs have been implicated in direct induction (Engelberth et al., 2004; Wang et al., 2023), and both GLVs and indole are known to prime defenses, and are thus considered as 'bioactive' in information transfer between plants (Erb et al., 2015; Hu et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Both GLVs and indole are known to prime defenses, and are thus considered as 'bioactive' in information transfer between plants.
source: In maize, GLVs have been implicated in direct induction (Engelberth et al., 2004; Wang et al., 2023), and both GLVs and indole are known to prime defenses, and are thus considered as 'bioactive' in information transfer between plants (Erb et al., 2015; Hu et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: In darkness, the emission of many volatiles, especially those released via stomata, is severely hindered.
source: In darkness, the emission of many volatiles, especially those released via stomata, is severely hindered (Seidl-Adams et al., 2015; He et al., 2021; Bläsing et al., 2005; Lin et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Within 3 hr of herbivore feeding, a small induction of sesquiterpenes, monoterpenes, DMNT, and TMTT was detected in undamaged receiver plants.
source: Herbivore feeding began around 12:00 and within 3 hr, we detected a small induction of sesquiterpenes [C15H25+, m/z=205.20], monoterpenes [C10H17+, m/z=137.13], 4,8-dimethylnona-1,3,7-triene (DMNT) [C11H19+, m/z=151.15], and 4,8,12-trimethyltrideca-1,3,7,11-tetraene (TMTT) [C16H27+, m/z=219.21] in undamaged receiver plants.
evidence: The claim is supported by PTR-ToF-MS measurements shown in Figure 1.

claim: Volatile emission was severely impaired during the night, regardless of treatment.
source: Volatile emission was severely impaired during the night, regardless of treatment.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1 showing reduced emissions during dark periods.

claim: As soon as the light was restored, a strong burst of terpene release from receiver plants was observed, which was two to five times higher than the release the day before.
source: Interestingly, as soon as the light was restored, we observed a strong burst of terpene release from receiver plants, which was two to five times higher than the release the day before (Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by PTR-ToF-MS data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Exposure to volatiles from a herbivore-attacked plant triggers a delayed burst in terpene emission in neighboring plants.
source: Thus, exposure to volatiles from a herbivore-attacked plant triggers a delayed burst in terpene emission in neighboring plants.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from PTR-ToF-MS measurements.

claim: During the night, plants close their stomata to limit water loss.
source: During the night, plants close their stomata to limit water loss (Caird et al., 2007), which may also impair terpene release, thus leading to an accumulation of terpenes in the leaves and a burst once stomata open again (Seidl-Adams et al., 2015; Loughrin et al., 1994).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Internal pools of β-caryophyllene, β-farnesene, and TMTT were marginally induced after 3 hr, but only became significantly induced after 8 hr of exposure to HIPVs.
source: Internal pools of β-caryophyllene, β-farnesene, and TMTT were marginally induced after 3 hr, but only became significantly induced after 8 hr of exposure to HIPVs (Figure 2A, B, and D, Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by measurements of internal terpene pools shown in Figure 2 and statistical analysis in Table 1.

claim: For β-caryophyllene, β-farnesene, and TMTT, accumulation remained higher during the night (16.75 hr) as well as the following day.
source: For all three, accumulation remained higher during the night (16.75 hr) as well as the following day.
evidence: The claim is supported by measurements shown in Figure 2.

claim: α-Bergamotene only began accumulating in leaves on the second day.
source: α-Bergamotene only began accumulating in leaves on the second day (Figure 2C, Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by measurements shown in Figure 2C and Table 1.

claim: Internal terpene pools remain comparable between night and day.
source: Thus, internal terpene pools remain comparable between night and day, suggesting that terpenes do not continue accumulating during the night and that, even when terpenes are emitted in large amounts on day 2, internal pools do not drop below nighttime levels.
evidence: The claim is supported by measurements of internal terpene pools over time.

claim: In maize, farnesene pyrophosphate synthase 3 (FPPS3), terpene synthase 2 and 10 (TPS2 and TPS10, respectively), as well as dimethylnonatriene/trimethyltetradecatetraene synthase (CYP92C5) are rate limiting for terpene production.
source: In maize, farnesene pyrophosphate synthase 3 (FPPS3), terpene synthase 2 and 10 (TPS2 and TPS10, respectively), as well as dimethylnonatriene/trimethyltetradecatetraene synthase (CYP92C5) are rate limiting for terpene production (Block et al., 2019; Richter et al., 2015; Richter et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: All terpene biosynthesis genes (FPPS3, TPS2, TPS10, CYP92C5) were induced by HIPV exposure during daytime, but not during the night.
source: All genes were induced by HIPV exposure during daytime, but not during the night.
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 2E-H.

claim: FPPS3 was slightly induced after 3 hr and significantly induced after 8 hr of HIPV exposure.
source: FPPS3 was slightly induced after 3 hr and significantly induced after 8 hr of HIPV exposure (Figure 2E, Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 2E and Table 1.

claim: TPS2 was slightly induced 3, 8, and 22 hr after the onset of HIPV exposure.
source: TPS2 was slightly induced 3, 8, and 22 hr after the onset of HIPV exposure (Figure 2F, Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 2F and Table 1.

claim: TPS10 was significantly induced after 3 and 22 hr of HIPV exposure.
source: TPS10 was significantly induced after 3 and 22 hr of HIPV exposure (Figure 2G, Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 2G and Table 1.

claim: CYP92C5 was only significantly induced after 3 hr of HIPV exposure.
source: CYP92C5 was only significantly induced after 3 hr of HIPV exposure (Figure 2H, Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 2H and Table 1.

claim: The patterns of volatile terpene biosynthesis do not support a scenario where the terpene burst on the second day is due to continued biosynthesis but lack of emission during the night.
source: The patterns of volatile terpene biosynthesis do not support a scenario where the terpene burst on the second day is due to continued biosynthesis but lack of emission during the night.
evidence: The claim is inferred from gene expression data showing no induction during the night.

claim: Volatile release in maize is regulated by jasmonates.
source: Volatile release in maize is regulated by jasmonates (Martin et al., 2003; Ament et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: A significant induction of OPDA and JA-Ile production as well as OPR7 expression was found at the beginning of the second day, 22 hr after the onset of volatile exposure.
source: We found a significant induction of OPDA and JA-Ile production as well as OPR7 expression at the beginning of the second day, 22 hr after the onset of volatile exposure (Figure 3, Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by phytohormone measurements and gene expression data shown in Figure 3 and Table 1.

claim: Jasmonate production is temporally aligned with the delayed terpene burst at the onset of the second day.
source: Thus, jasmonate production is temporally aligned with the delayed terpene burst at the onset of the second day.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the temporal correlation between jasmonate and terpene measurements.

claim: Under continuous light, the largest burst of terpene emission occurred ca. 12–18 hr after the onset of volatile exposure.
source: Similar to exposure during a normal light regime, the largest burst of terpene emission occurred ca. 12–18 hr after the onset of volatile exposure (Figure 4), suggesting that the temporal delay in volatile emission in receiver plants is not dependent on light fluctuations, but is otherwise clocked.
evidence: The claim is supported by PTR-ToF-MS data from continuous light experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: The temporal delay in volatile emission in receiver plants is not dependent on light fluctuations, but is otherwise clocked.
source: Similar to exposure during a normal light regime, the largest burst of terpene emission occurred ca. 12–18 hr after the onset of volatile exposure (Figure 4), suggesting that the temporal delay in volatile emission in receiver plants is not dependent on light fluctuations, but is otherwise clocked.
evidence: The claim is inferred from continuous light experiments showing similar delayed burst patterns.

claim: When herbivory treatment started around 20:00 hr under continuous light, a terpene burst was observed 10–12 hr after HIPV exposure.
source: However, instead of starting the herbivory treatment at ca. 12:00 hr, we started it around 20:00 hr. Similarly, we observed an initial bump in terpene emission followed by a larger burst 10–12 hr after HIPV exposure (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: In both continuous light experiments the 'second day' burst occurred somewhat earlier than under normal light conditions.
source: In both continuous light experiments the 'second day' burst occurred somewhat earlier than under normal light conditions.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of data from continuous light and normal light experiments.

claim: Stomata, which are closed in the dark, may delay the onset of the terpene burst under dark:light transitions.
source: It is possible that stomata, which are closed in the dark, delay the onset of the terpene burst under dark:light transitions.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning based on stomatal behavior.

claim: Strong positive correlations were found between hexenyl acetate, hexenal, hexen-1-ol, and indole emissions in sender plants and terpene responses in receiver plants when plants had a dark period.
source: We found strong positive correlations between hexenyl acetate, hexenal, hexen-1-ol, and indole emissions in sender plants and terpene responses in receiver plants when plants had a dark period (Figure 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: Under continuous light, the apex of bioactive volatile emission in sender plants was not temporally aligned with the apex of terpene responses in receiver plants.
source: Interestingly, this was not the case under continuous light, where the apex of bioactive volatile emission in sender plants was not temporally aligned with the apex of terpene responses in receiver plants (Figure 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: Sender plant emissions showed slight negative correlations with terpene induction in receiver plants under continuous light.
source: Sender plant emissions even showed slight negative correlations with terpene induction in receiver plants under continuous light.
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: The emission kinetics of bioactive volatiles from sender plants cannot fully explain the delayed terpene burst.
source: Thus, the emission kinetics of bioactive volatiles from sender plants cannot fully explain the delayed terpene burst.
evidence: The claim is inferred from correlation analysis showing lack of alignment under continuous light.

claim: Following short exposure to HIPVs, a generally small, but significant, induction of sesquiterpenes, monoterpenes, DMNT, and TMTT emissions was detected in receiver plants.
source: Following the short exposure to HIPVs, we detected a generally small, but significant, induction of sesquiterpenes, monoterpenes, DMNT, and TMTT emissions in receiver plants (Figure 7, Table 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by PTR-ToF-MS data shown in Figure 7 and statistical analysis in Table 2.

claim: At the beginning of the next day, a slight induction in terpene emissions was found, most apparent for sesquiterpenes and TMTT, in plants that had been exposed to herbivory-induced volatiles 18 hr prior.
source: At the beginning of the next day, we found a slight induction in terpene emissions, most apparent for sesquiterpenes and TMTT, in plants that had been exposed to herbivory-induced volatiles 18 hr prior (Figure 7, Table 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by PTR-ToF-MS data shown in Figure 7 and statistical analysis in Table 2.

claim: HAC exposure at the beginning of the next day induced terpene emissions.
source: HAC exposure at the beginning of the next day also induced terpene emissions.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7.

claim: HAC induced a stronger release of all terpenes in plants that had been exposed to HIPVs the previous day.
source: Furthermore, HAC induced a stronger release of all terpenes in plants that had been exposed to HIPVs the previous day.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7 showing interaction effects.

claim: Induction in terpene emission by HAC was similar regardless of whether induction began 30 min or 4 hr 30 min after lights came on.
source: We exposed maize seedlings to HAC dispensers either 30 min or 4 hr 30 min after lights came on. We found induction in terpene emission to be similar regardless of when induction began (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Exposure to HIPVs prompts maize plants to release more terpenes the next day.
source: Thus, exposure to HIPVs prompts maize plants to release more terpenes the next day and also primes maize plants to respond more strongly to a secondary HIPV trigger.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data showing delayed terpene induction.

claim: Exposure to HIPVs primes maize plants to respond more strongly to a secondary HIPV trigger.
source: Thus, exposure to HIPVs prompts maize plants to release more terpenes the next day and also primes maize plants to respond more strongly to a secondary HIPV trigger.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data showing enhanced response to HAC after HIPV priming.

claim: The combination of delayed terpene release and priming results in a pronounced terpene burst.
source: Together, these two phenomena result in a pronounced terpene burst.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data showing both priming and direct induction effects.

claim: More natural continuous exposure to volatiles results in the same priming pattern without the need for another stimulus.
source: Our findings demonstrate that more natural continuous exposure to volatiles results in the same pattern without the need for another stimulus.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data comparing continuous exposure to short-term exposure.

claim: HIPVs are sufficient to trigger robust, clocked defense activation in neighboring plants.
source: We thus conclude that HIPVs are sufficient to trigger robust, clocked defense activation in neighboring plants.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: On day 1, maize plants are exposed to GLVs, which trigger a small burst of terpene release in receiver plants.
source: On day 1, maize plants are exposed to GLVs, which trigger a small burst of terpene release in receiver plants.
evidence: The claim is part of a mechanistic scenario inferred from experimental data.

claim: Receiver plants are primed to respond more strongly on the next day, once light is restored.
source: At the same time, receiver plants are primed to respond more strongly on the next day, once light is restored.
evidence: The claim is part of a mechanistic scenario inferred from experimental data.

claim: At the onset of the second day, the emission of GLVs from the neighboring plants increases.
source: At the onset of the second day, four things happen simultaneously. First, the emission of GLVs from the neighboring plants increases.
evidence: The claim is part of a mechanistic scenario inferred from sender plant volatile emission data.

claim: At the onset of the second day, the defense priming mechanism responding to GLV cues kicks into gear.
source: Second, the defense priming mechanism responding to these cues kicks into gear.
evidence: The claim is part of a mechanistic scenario inferred from priming experiments.

claim: At the onset of the second day, terpene production is activated.
source: Third, terpene production is activated.
evidence: The claim is part of a mechanistic scenario inferred from gene expression and terpene accumulation data.

claim: At the onset of the second day, stomata open and enable volatile emission.
source: Fourth, stomata open and enable volatile emission.
evidence: The claim is part of a mechanistic scenario based on established knowledge of stomatal behavior.

claim: The orchestration of GLV emission increase, priming activation, terpene production, and stomatal opening results in a strong terpene burst.
source: Together, these elements result in a strong terpene burst.
evidence: The claim is a synthesis of the mechanistic scenario inferred from experimental data.

claim: Considering we observed an induction in jasmonates coinciding with terpene bursts it is likely that non-volatile jasmonate-dependent defenses follow similar temporal patterns.
source: Additionally, considering we observed an induction in jasmonates coinciding with terpene bursts it is likely that non-volatile jasmonate-dependent defenses follow similar temporal patterns.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning based on observed jasmonate induction patterns.

claim: Responding most strongly to volatile cues on the second day may avoid unnecessary energy expenditure.
source: First, responding most strongly to volatile cues on the second day may avoid unnecessary energy expenditure (Waterman et al., 2019; Mithöfer et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis about ecological relevance supported by citations.

claim: GLVs are emitted upon both herbivore attack and mechanical damage.
source: GLVs are emitted upon both herbivore attack and mechanical damage (Gardiner et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: When damage is not sustained, GLVs will dissipate rapidly.
source: However, when damage is not sustained, GLVs will dissipate rapidly (D'Auria et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Responding most strongly to repeated GLV exposure could avoid false negatives and allow plants to respond more robustly to the presence of actual herbivory.
source: Thus, responding most strongly to repeated GLV exposure could avoid false negatives and allow plants to respond more robustly to the presence of actual herbivory.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning about adaptive benefits.

claim: Sending out volatiles on the second day may maximize indirect defenses.
source: Second, sending out volatiles on the second day may maximize indirect defenses.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis about ecological relevance.

claim: Attracting natural enemies too early to herbivore-free plants could have fitness costs for both the plant and herbivore natural enemies.
source: Attracting natural enemies too early to herbivore-free plants could have fitness costs for both the plant and herbivore natural enemies.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning about ecological costs.

claim: Responding on the second day could be advantageous, as by this time, the natural enemies would have located and interacted with the herbivores on sender plants, and would thus be ready to move over to the next plant in anticipation of herbivore arrival.
source: Responding on the second day could be advantageous, as by this time, the natural enemies would have located and interacted with the herbivores on sender plants, and would thus be ready to move over to the next plant in anticipation of herbivore arrival.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning about ecological advantages.

claim: HIPVs also attract herbivores.
source: As fitness outcomes are likely highly nuanced, especially considering HIPVs also attract herbivores (Zu et al., 2020), investigation into information transfer on the multi-plant scale, namely in the context of multi-trophic interactions, will be critical.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: V2-stage Zea mays (maize, B73) was used throughout this study.
source: V2-stage Zea mays (maize, B73) was used throughout this study.
evidence: The claim is a methodological statement.

claim: At V2 stage, maize has four leaves: two are fully developed, one is expanding and one is emerging.
source: At this stage, maize has four leaves: two are fully developed, one is expanding and one is emerging.
evidence: The claim is a description of plant developmental stage.

claim: S. exigua were reared from eggs on artificial diet and used for experiments when they reached the fourth instar stage.
source: S. exigua (Frontier Agricultural Sciences, USA) were reared from eggs on artificial diet (Maag et al., 2014) and used for experiments when they reached the fourth instar stage.
evidence: The claim is a methodological statement.

claim: The herbivore treatment consisted of adding 3 fourth instar larvae onto plants (sender plants).
source: The herbivore treatment consisted of adding 3 fourth instar larvae onto plants (sender plants).
evidence: The claim is a methodological statement.

claim: HAC dispensers emitted HAC at a rate of 4.68 (±0.40 SD) nmol hr–1.
source: HAC dispensers emitted HAC at a rate of 4.68 (±0.40 SD) nmol hr–1 and maize seedlings infested with 3 fourth instar S. exigua larvae emitted all GLVs at a rate of 1.94 nmol hr–1 (±0.25 SD).
evidence: The claim is supported by measurements of dispenser emission rates.

claim: Maize seedlings infested with 3 fourth instar S. exigua larvae emitted all GLVs at a rate of 1.94 nmol hr–1 (±0.25 SD).
source: HAC dispensers emitted HAC at a rate of 4.68 (±0.40 SD) nmol hr–1 and maize seedlings infested with 3 fourth instar S. exigua larvae emitted all GLVs at a rate of 1.94 nmol hr–1 (±0.25 SD).
evidence: The claim is supported by measurements of plant GLV emission rates.

claim: GLV emissions induced by caterpillars vary over time, and can be more than twofold higher than the average during times of strong active feeding.
source: Of note, GLV emissions induced by caterpillars vary over time, and can be more than twofold higher than the average during times of strong active feeding (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: The release rate of the HAC dispensers is within the plant's physiological range.
source: Thus, the release rate of the dispensers is within the plant's physiological range.
evidence: The claim is inferred from comparison of dispenser and plant emission rates.

claim: Terpenes are not known to prime or induce volatile release in maize.
source: Terpenes are not known to prime or induce volatile release in maize, and were thus not included in the sender plant analysis (Ruther and Fürstenau, 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: In maize, GLVs directly induce and prime jasmonate production and terpene release.
source: In maize, GLVs directly induce and prime jasmonate production and terpene release (Hu et al., 2019; Engelberth et al., 2004; Wang et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Indole can prime, but not directly induce jasmonate production and terpene release.
source: Indole can prime, but not directly induce these two responses (Erb et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: GLVs and indole can interact to increase defense priming upon a secondary stimulus.
source: GLVs and indole again can interact to increase defense priming upon a secondary stimulus (Hu et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: β-caryophyllene is a minor sesquiterpene in B73.
source: This type of variation was not visible in total sesquiterpene emissions measured by proton transfer reaction time-of-flight mass spectrometry (PTR-ToF-MS) (Figure 1), likely because β-caryophyllene is a minor sesquiterpene in B73 (Block et al., 2018) and closed stomata block sesquiterpene emission at night (Seidl-Adams et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Closed stomata block sesquiterpene emission at night.
source: This type of variation was not visible in total sesquiterpene emissions measured by proton transfer reaction time-of-flight mass spectrometry (PTR-ToF-MS) (Figure 1), likely because β-caryophyllene is a minor sesquiterpene in B73 (Block et al., 2018) and closed stomata block sesquiterpene emission at night (Seidl-Adams et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: OPR7 is critical for JA biosynthesis.
source: To understand whether the delayed terpene burst is associated with jasmonate signaling, we measured the levels of 12-oxo-phytodienoic acid (OPDA), jasmonic acid (JA), and jasmonic acid-isoleucine (JA-Ile), as well as the expression of oxo-phytodienoate reductase 7 (OPR7), which is critical for JA biosynthesis (Yan et al., 2012).
